content.text:
**Finding: compliant** — no redline proposed.

**What I checked.** I searched the whole agreement for restrictive-covenant language ("compete", "Exclusivity", "shall not develop", "Sanofi shall not / will not", "its Affiliates shall not", "restriction") and read the Term and Termination article, the covenants article, and the assignment/change-of-control provisions in full.

**Conclusion.** There is no non-compete, exclusivity or field-of-use covenant binding Sanofi, which is the playbook's *preferred* position:

- The only covenants running against Sanofi are the mutual debarment, compliance and pharmacovigilance covenants in Section 13.4; Section 13.3's substantive covenants bind RevMed alone.
- "Field" is defined as "any and all uses" (p0053), so there is no field limitation on us, and Section 3.8 expressly says neither Party must "agree to any restrictions on the businesses of RevMed or Sanofi or its Affiliates" to obtain antitrust clearance (p0271) — a provision that works in our favour.
- The restraint flagged by the planner, Section 12.2(d), is **not a prohibition**. Sanofi stays free to develop, manufacture or commercialize a Competing Product; the sole consequence is a RevMed termination right that arises only after a stated period, is unavailable once Sanofi has commenced a Registrational Clinical Trial for a Product, operates during the Term only with no post-term tail, and can be defeated by a Sanofi written election. That is softer than even the fallback.
- The Section 12.3(c) reversion/transition consequences are the same package that applies to Sanofi's own termination for convenience, so they are not an incremental competitive restraint and are better addressed (if at all) under the termination-consequences rules.
- The Section 15.2 separation conditions (A)–(D) attach to the **RevMed**-as-acquired-Party case (p0613/p0614); for Sanofi, p0612 excludes acquirer IP and the Acquiror Family unconditionally — again favourable to us, so not flagged.

**Noted, not flagged.** Two points short of an ideal draft: the "Competing Product" definition (p0037) is redacted so its breadth can't be fully verified, and Section 12.2(d) has no express internal-development or acquisition carve-out. Since 12.2(d) creates only a termination right rather than a covenant, neither restricts our business, so no redline is warranted. If the redacted "Competing Product" scope turns out to be materially broader than SHP2 inhibitors, that is worth a look at diligence.
